newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda refugees flee in crossfire in Zaire - U.N..
newsitem.headline: Rwanda refugees flee in crossfire in Zaire - U.N..

text.p: Some 200,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees fled a camp in eastern Zaire and were caught in crossfire on Friday between Tutsi rebels and Zairean troops, a U.N. aid worker said.

"Katale (camp) is empty. The refugees say that they are on the run and caught in the crossfire," Michele Quintaglie of the World Food Programe (WFP) told Reuters by telephone from the airean city of Goma.

She said Katale camp, 45 km (28 miles) north of the North Kivu provincial capital of Goma, had held 210,000 refugees. It was the largest refugee camp in eastern Zaire before two weeks of fighting uprooted more than half a million refugees.
The refugees are Rwandan Hutus and the rebels are Tutsis.
Quintaglie said she did not know where the refugees were heading, but she guessed it might be towards the southwest. Mugunga camp, the largest in the world, is in that direction.
Quintaglie also said the 107 foreign aid workers in Goma were told to gather at concentration points in the city on Friday for possible evacuation from eastern Zaire.
Earlier on Friday, Goma, which suffered fierce battles on its fringes pitting Zairean troops and former Rwandan Hutu soldiers against Tutsi rebels on Thursday, was quieter.
From the Rwandan border, I saw 12 rockets fired from multiple rocket launchers land between five and 10 km (three to six miles) north of Goma airport early on Friday followed by sporadic arms fire.

At the Zaire-Rwanda border crossing, the atmosphere on Friday morning was surreal. Five Zairean soldiers at the border post danced naked, waving automatic weapons, chanting and sprinkling water on each other.
Goma is the administrative centre for relief operations for 1.1. million Rwandan Hutu refugees, 200,000 Burundians and tens of thousands of Zaireans fleeing the fighting in eastern Zaire.
Many of them have been on the run from fighting for at least a week amid fears they will be hit by hunger and epidemics.

The refugees now live in a constant state of panic. "At one point yesterday we had refugees on the road walking in both directions," said Panos Moumtzis, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR).
"They are really panicking. They are very scared. They do not know where to go," he added from his office in Goma city.
Zaire on Thursday defiantly rejected peace talks with its neighbours despite fears that victories by advancing ethnic Tutsi rebels could herald the disintegration of the vast Central African nation.

The conflict in eastern Zaire assumed greater international dimensions with the Kinshasa government adding Uganda to the list of its enemies and more world leaders urging round table peace negotiations.

"The government will not undertake any negotiation, will not participate in any regional conference while a part of national territory is occupied by foreign forces," Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo told an emergency parliament session on Thursday.

"This war which the combined forces of Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda are waging against Zaire has brought to broad daylight Rwanda's intention not to welcome on its territory its nationals living in Zaire and to pursue its insane plan of annexing a part of our territory."
Foreign armies have denied fighting alongside Tutsi rebels in Zaire but Rwanda has said it sent troops on an incursion this week after artillery and machinegun exchanges across its border.
The new United Nations envoy to Central Africa, Raymond Chretien, said he would focus on securing a ceasefire before tackling any other problems in the growing crisis.
"A great urgency exists because of the fighting that is taking place in the region. Only after a ceasefire will it be possible to tackle the humanitarian crisis," he told reporters.
The Canadian diplomat plans to begin his mission shortly and said his first stop would be Lausanne, Switzerland, to see Zairean ruler Mobutu Sese Seko, who is undergoing cancer treatment there.
Chretien also intends to speak to leaders of surrounding countries, especially Rwanda, and attempt to see local leaders in eastern Zaire.

Kenyan state radio said Kenya planned to host a summit of seven African countries on November 5 but did not say if the main subject would be the war in eastern Zaire, where Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels have seized a string of towns.

France, the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) called for talks to resolve a conflict threatening the lives of refugees who fled to Zaire to escape ethnic strife in Rwanda and Burundi.
